Under this strategy, the Company intends to monetize select real estate assets through asset sales and joint ventures, which may include the sale of interests in certain operating assets and the formation of joint ventures for portions of its residential MPC land holdings.
The Company expects HHC to retain operational control of these assets and to continue to serve as developer, manager, and operator under long-term agreements.

The Company also intends to raise third-party capital to fund future development, with HHC earning development, asset management, and performance fees, including as general partner of new real estate funds or other third-party capital vehicles.
The Company expects to maintain its existing approach for its condominium developments, which are primarily funded through construction financing and buyer deposits.

Short-Term Liquidity In the next 12 months, we expect to continue to drive meaningful value creation following our transition to a diversified holding company.

From our real estate operations, we expect our primary sources of cash in the next 12 months to include cash flow from MPC land sales and condominium closings, cash generated from our operating assets, first mortgage financings secured by our assets, and deposits from condominium sales (which are restricted to funding construction of the related developments).

In connection with the planned transition of HHC to an asset-light real estate development and asset management platform as described above, we also expect our sources of cash to potentially include proceeds from the sale of interests in select operating assets, the disposition of non-core assets, and the formation of joint ventures for portions of our residential MPC land holdings and, over time, development,…

We expect our primary uses of cash to include condominium pre-development and development costs, debt principal payments and debt service costs, MPC land development costs, other strategic developments costs, and general operating costs.
To the extent the planned monetization transactions are completed, we expect our uses of cash to also include transaction costs and the potential repayment of debt secured by the related assets.

From our insurance operations, we expect our primary sources of cash to include premiums collected from policyholders, investment income earned from our investment portfolio, recoveries from reinsurers, proceeds from the sale or maturity of investments, and if needed, available borrowings under Vantage’s revolving credit facility.
We expect our primary uses of cash to include payment of claims, premiums ceded to reinsurers, commissions and other policy acquisition costs, and general operating expenses.

We believe that our sources of cash, including existing cash on hand, will provide sufficient liquidity to meet our existing obligations and anticipated ordinary course operating expenses for at least the next 12 months.
Long-Term Liquidity We expect our long-term sources and uses of cash for our real estate and insurance operations to continue to align with those mentioned above.

To the extent we implement the planned transition of our real estate operations to an asset-light real estate development and asset management platform, cash generated from our Operating Assets and MPC land sales is expected to decrease in relation to any interests sold, while development, asset management, and performance fees may partially offset this decrease over time.
We also expect that third-party capital partners may fund a potentially substantial portion of our future development.
For our insurance operations, we expect cash inflows to grow over time through the optimization of underwriting profitability and investment strategies.
The Company’s investment strategy is managed to establish a level of cash, investments, and expected future cash flow that will be able to meet foreseeable payment obligations.

The timing and amount of the payments under insurance and reinsurance contracts are contingent upon the outcome of future events and actual payments will likely vary, perhaps materially, from any forecasted payments, as well as from the liabilities recorded in our Condensed Consolidated Balance Sheets.
We anticipate that these payments will be funded by operating cash flows.

The preparation of financial statements in accordance with GAAP requires management to make informed judgments, assumptions, and estimates that affect the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses.
They comprise (i) case reserves for claims that have been reported to us and (ii) reserves for losses incurred but not reported (IBNR), which also reflect expected development on reported claims.

Methodology In establishing these reserves, management considers claim-specific information, historical loss experience, actuarial analyses, and other relevant information, including expected loss ratios, reported and paid loss development patterns, claim frequency and severity trends, underwriting and pricing information, business mix, policy terms and conditions, cedent and broker information, industry data,…

Management employs multiple actuarial methods to estimate ultimate losses, including the paid and reported (incurred) loss development (chain ladder) methods, the paid and reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson methods, frequency and severity methods, and the expected loss ratio method.
If a quantitative sensitivity to a reasonably likely change in a significant assumption becomes material and reasonably available, we will disclose the estimated effect of that change.
